problem: Existing ObjectNav benchmarks fix the goal set to 6-21 categories (HM3D, MP3D) or use synthetic scenes (ProcTHOR, OVMM). They only test generalization to new scenes, not to new goal categories given in free-form language. It is also unclear which training recipes work best for open-vocabulary ObjectNav: IL vs RL, BC vs DAgger, shortest-path vs exploration demos, RNN vs transformer.
motivation: Real assistant robots must find arbitrary, language-specified objects in real homes, so a benchmark is needed that tests generalization across degrees of semantic novelty in the goal category. The authors observe that end-to-end policies degrade sharply on unseen categories. A modular map-plus-open-vocabulary-detector method (VLFM) stays roughly constant across splits but is brittle to odometry and actuation noise, which motivates combining the two.
key_idea: The paper builds HM3D-OVON, a large open-vocabulary ObjectNav benchmark on HM3DSem real-world scans. It has three evaluation splits of increasing semantic distance from the training categories (Val Seen / Val Seen Synonyms / Val Unseen). It then benchmarks IL, RL and modular agents on it, and proposes DAgRL+OD: a DAgger-then-RL transformer policy that explores, plus an open-vocabulary detector and a PointNav policy for bee-lining to the detected goal.
insight: (1) Training recipe matters. DAgger with a fast online frontier-exploration expert beats offline BC (Table I: 18.1 vs 11.1 SR on Val Seen). Frontier-exploration demos beat shortest-path demos (DAgRL 41.3 vs 37.7 SR, Table III), which contradicts SPOC's finding; the authors attribute this to HM3D scans being more cluttered and complex than ProcTHOR. Transformers beat LSTMs when data is diverse, i.e. DAgger/RL (DAgRL 41.3 vs 36.5; RL 39.2 vs 32.9, Table IV), but not with static BC data. (2) End-to-end policies learn exploration well but do not generalize recognition to semantically novel categories: DAgRL falls from 41.3 to 29.4 to 18.3 SR across the splits. Failure analysis shows this is mostly from ignoring the visible goal (2.6%→8.6%→16.8%) and leaving the success region (2.2%→11.4%→17.8%), not from worse exploration. Plugging in an OWLv2 detector plus a PointNav bee-line fixes this (37.1 SR on Val Unseen). (3) Because the exploration policy is RGB-only and map-free, it is nearly insensitive to test-time odometry and actuation noise (SR drops ≤0.3), whereas map-based VLFM loses up to 6.1 SR.
method: HM3D-OVON dataset: episodes are built from HM3DSem dense annotations with no scene or instance overlap between splits. There are 145 train scenes (50k episodes each, 7.25M episodes) and 36 val scenes (3k episodes each). Goals must occupy ≥5% of the Stretch camera view from some vantage point within 1 m. Start positions are on the same floor as a goal, with a geodesic distance of 1-30 m.

Semantic evaluation splits: about 25% of categories are held out. Using SentenceBERT, a held-out category's maximum cosine similarity to the training categories decides its split: Val Seen Synonyms ([0.68, 0.96], 50 categories) or Val Unseen ([0.45, 0.68], 49 categories). Val Seen uses training categories in novel scenes.

Task/agent: Stretch-like embodiment (1.41 m tall, 17 cm radius, 360×640 RGB-D camera at 1.31 m). Actions are FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN L/R 30°, LOOK UP/DOWN 30°, and STOP. Success means calling STOP within 1 m of a goal within 500 steps.

Policy architecture: frozen SigLIP image and text encoders (768-d each) plus a 32-d previous-action embedding feed a 4-layer decoder-only transformer (8 heads, hidden size 512, context of 100 steps). A linear action head outputs the action, and a critic head is added for RL. An LSTM variant with a matched parameter count is used for ablation.

Fast frontier-exploration expert: frontier exploration followed by a shortest-path bee-line once the goal is within 3.5 m. It runs at about 1 ms/step versus about 250 ms in prior implementations, which enables online DAgger labeling instead of offline BC datasets.

Training recipes: BC, DAgger, and PPO RL with a dense distance-to-goal reward (r_success=2.5, slack -0.01; 300M steps). Also BCRL and DAgRL: 150M steps of IL pretraining followed by 150M steps of PPO fine-tuning with sparse reward (PIRLNav-style), trained with VER on 8 TITAN Xp GPUs.

DAgRL+OD: the DAgRL policy explores until an OWLv2 open-vocabulary detector fires on the goal. Control then switches to a pretrained depth+odometry PointNav policy (the same one VLFM uses), which navigates to the detected object and calls STOP.

setting.model_size: not stated (policy: 4-layer transformer, hidden 512, 8 heads; SigLIP 768-d embeddings)
setting.training_data: HM3D-OVON train split: 145 HM3DSem scenes, 50k episodes/scene (~7.25M episodes). Online frontier-exploration expert labels for DAgger (150M steps), then 150M steps of PPO with sparse reward. The BC ablation uses 7.25M offline trajectories per trajectory type (frontier / shortest path).
setting.observation: Exploration policy uses egocentric RGB + goal category text + previous action only; the +OD variant's detector and PointNav bee-lining additionally use depth + odometry
setting.action_space: discrete: MOVE_FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN_LEFT/RIGHT 30°, LOOK_UP/DOWN 30°, STOP
setting.privileged: none at test time (GT expert labels only during training)

numbers_note: HM3D-OVON has three evaluation splits: Val Seen, Val Seen Synonyms and Val Unseen, all in novel scenes. Val Seen Synonyms has no canonical split name and is logged here as split 'val', with the real name given in 'extra'. Results are means over 3 seeds; ± std values are omitted. Tables III and IV (trajectory type and RNN vs transformer ablations) report Val Seen only; e.g., DAgRL with shortest-path demos gets 37.7/19.0 and the RNN DAgRL gets 36.5/16.7. The failure-mode breakdown appears only in a figure. The dataset's total category, instance and scene counts are LaTeX macros that are not expanded in the source; the stated scene counts are 145 train and 36 val.
results: On HM3D-OVON, the end-to-end DAgRL policy is the best end-to-end method on Val Seen (41.3 SR / 21.2 SPL, beating VLFM's 35.2/18.6). However, it collapses on novel categories (29.4 SR on Val Seen Synonyms, 18.3 on Val Unseen), where VLFM with OWLv2 holds 32.4-35.2 SR. DAgRL+OD beats VLFM on all three splits (38.5/39.0/37.1 SR vs 35.2/32.4/35.2). Under test-time odometry and actuation noise it keeps 36.9-38.9 SR, while VLFM drops to 28.5-29.1.
limitations: End-to-end policies trained only on ObjectNav fail to generalize recognition to semantically novel categories. Good unseen-category performance relies on an external detector (OWLv2) trained on a far larger vocabulary that may overlap the evaluation categories.

Evaluation is simulation-only (Stretch-like agent in Habitat) with no real-robot experiments. Goals are object category names rather than rich free-form descriptions, despite the motivating example ('L-shaped couch').
Large failure modes remain across all splits: stopping at the wrong object and never seeing the goal, each about 17-20% of episodes. Training is expensive (300M environment steps).
